title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Lenox Twp pushes back on secret data center deals over power, noise and farmland.

lines.text: Good evening, and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Tonight we're diving into Lenox Township, where residents just learned through back channels about proposed data centers and they're demanding real answers.
That's right, Graham. This feels like the latest flashpoint in a statewide pushback over how these projects get approved.
Exactly. Let's start with what's happening right now in Lenox, out in Macomb County.
Residents there are upset they only found out about the plans through unofficial channels, not through official township notices.
They're worried about noise from the servers, the strain on the local power grid, and losing prime farmland to these massive facilities.
It sounds like a trust issue has built up fast. What do we know about how long this has been in the works?
The story broke today, but these kinds of proposals often simmer for months before they surface publicly.
And transparency failures like this are feeding distrust in local leadership across several counties.
Right. We've seen similar fights in places like Mason and even recalls tied directly to rezoning votes.
So how does this one in Lenox fit into the bigger pattern of communities trying to slow things down?
It's part of a wave where townships are using moratoriums and public pressure to buy time for better rules.
What kind of power demand are we talking about here? These facilities can be huge.
Hundreds of megawatts in some cases, which is why utilities are already planning major upgrades that ratepayers would ultimately fund.
And that ties straight into the new filing we saw today about doubling capacity statewide.
Yes, and folks 30 or 60 miles away could see higher bills even if the data center isn't in their backyard.
Water use is another big one, right? Cooling these places takes a lot.
It does, and that's why Zeeland Township just put a year-long pause on both data centers and related power projects.
They heard the same concerns about noise, water, and tax breaks that Lenox residents are raising now.
Ypsilanti extended its own moratorium for the same reasons — studying impacts on rates and supply.
And one township is even using a six-month power connection freeze to block a project linked to U-M and Los Alamos.
That shows local governments still have real tools to slow hyperscale builds even after bigger interests get involved.
What happens next in Lenox specifically? Are residents organizing petitions or recalls like elsewhere?
They're pushing for full disclosure first, but the recall attempts in Mason and the failed one tied to rezoning show how these fights can escalate quickly.
A second recall bid failed today in another community over data center rezoning, so the bar is high.
Voters 30 miles away are watching these disputes because the outcomes shape what developers can do in neighboring areas.
Ionia is also weighing whether to let data centers tap city power and land, with no vote yet but the door clearly open.
That conversation signals more communities are at least entertaining the idea despite the risks to local bills.
Meanwhile a state bill from yesterday could limit those tax abatements developers rely on.
Towns have used those breaks to attract projects, but if they go away, residents might face higher local taxes or fewer incentives.
And there's the report on Congressman John James voting against letting localities keep more control.
Those votes matter because so many communities are now facing proposals with big power and water demands.
So the tension between state-level interest and local pushback is only growing.
It is. And the ratepayer impact filing from the utility makes clear that upgrades will be needed wherever growth happens.
Graham, how many townships have similar pauses or reviews in place right now?
At least a handful we know of — Zeeland, Ypsilanti, and that one using the power freeze — and more are watching.
It feels like a patchwork approach while bigger policy questions linger.
Exactly. And farmland loss is a real concern in places like Lenox where ag land is still productive.
Noise complaints from existing facilities elsewhere have residents nervous about what 24/7 operations would sound like.
All of which feeds back into why transparency matters so much — people want a say before decisions are locked in.
What do you think the township board's next move will be?
They'll likely face more pressure for public meetings and full disclosure on any proposals.
And if that doesn't happen, we could see organized opposition grow like in Mason.
The second recall attempt there failed, but the effort shows residents aren't giving up.
So the big story here is really about trust and process as much as the projects themselves.
It is. And that sets the stage for everything else happening across the state today.
Let's move to quick hits. Graham, what's the latest on Ionia?
Council members there discussed inviting large facilities that could pull hundreds of megawatts, with no vote taken yet.
Residents 30 miles away could see higher bills if new plants or lines are needed.
Now over to Mason, where a recall drive launched today against the mayor over rezoning.
Petitioners say the changes went through without enough input, and it's the second attempt in recent months.
Zeeland Township approved a full-year moratorium on data centers and energy projects.
After hearing concerns on noise, water, and tax breaks — giving planners time for permanent rules.
Ypsilanti extended its moratorium while studying power rates and water supply impacts.
That keeps the status quo as surrounding townships consider their own limits.
One township deployed a six-month power freeze specifically to stall a U-M and Los Alamos linked project.
Showing how locals can slow things even after state-level interest surfaces.
A state bill from yesterday could end tax breaks for new data centers.
That would change how towns lure projects and could affect local taxes or incentives.
And a report shows Congressman John James voted four times against local control measures.
Those votes could matter in competitive districts come midterms.
Now for on deck — any major meetings listeners should know about?
Nothing formally scheduled in the next day or two from what we're tracking, but keep watching township boards.
Several places are still in the middle of moratorium reviews and public comment periods.
So residents should check their local agendas for any last-minute additions.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Lenox Twp Residents Demand Full Disclosure on Hidden Data Center Plans
